A novel approach for automatically identifying and outlining neoplasms in the esophagus using CT scans has been developed. The proposed DDAUnet model integrates the principles of dense connectivity and focus loss to effectively handle the complex patterns and boundaries of esophageal tumors. To account for the esophagus's variable shape and the presence of air-filled cavities within the scan data, a multi-scale, fully convolutional atlas-to-image regression technique called Atlas-Net was employed to create a detailed, 3D atlas of the esophagus. This atlas was then utilized to define a region of interest and guide the segmentation process. The evaluation of the proposed method on two publicly available datasets demonstrated its superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art techniques. The development of the DDAUnet model and the atlas generation technique are available on GitHub at https://github.com/IBM/DDAUnet. The model's efficiency was evaluated on a Tesla V100 GPU, with an inference time of 0.25 seconds per slice. The proposed method has been applied in a clinical setting at the Columbia University Medical Center. Reinforcement learning agents can excel at optimizing complex policies, but they often struggle to adapt to new situations outside their training environment. To overcome this limitation, agents are often trained on a diverse set of environments, known as a "spectrum" of related tasks. Experience replay buffers are a valuable tool for enhancing the performance of agents in new environments, by providing a pool of previously collected data that can be re-used to improve the policy. However, the effectiveness of experience replay is hindered by its inability to adapt to new situations, as it prioritizes data based on the same criteria regardless of the target environment. In this paper, we introduce a novel experience replay framework that dynamically adjusts the variance of the data distribution to match the target environment, thereby enhancing the performance of agents in new situations. We demonstrate the superiority of our approach on a range of continuous control tasks, including challenging scenarios with a large spectrum of related tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengzhengwu/vedere.

In recent years, the development of large-scale conversational agents has been significantly influenced by the creation of end-to-end dialogue systems without the need for extensive training data. These systems have shown the potential to engage users in dynamic conversations with multiple turns. However, the current state-of-the-art models are limited in their ability to handle complex conversations with multiple branches, a common occurrence in real-world scenarios. To address this challenge, researchers have explored the use of memory-augmented models, specifically attention-based neural Turing machines and external memory, to manage the flow of conversations. In response to these advancements, we present a novel approach called MultiTalk, a highly-branching dialogue framework that leverages the strengths of both memory-augmented models and neural networks to manage conversations. This system enables the creation of diverse conversations with multiple branches, allowing the agent to explore different topics and engage in more dynamic discussions. To evaluate the effectiveness of MultiTalk, we developed a custom dataset featuring conversations with multiple branches, and the system's performance was also compared to a baseline model using the existing ConvAI2 dataset. The results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed framework in managing complex conversations and its ability to engage users in more varied and dynamic discussions. The system's code and the specially designed dataset are available for public use.

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has been operating at unprecedented energy levels, allowing for the study of fundamental interactions and the search for new physics beyond the Standard Model. As a result, there is a growing need for advanced theoretical tools to interpret and make predictions from LHC data. The growing need for real-time audio and speech processing in applications like voice assistants, live video conferencing, and online gaming has created a pressing issue for developers: ensuring seamless, lag-free experience without compromising security updates. However, the rising prevalence of hardware mitigations against Spectre attacks has significantly slowed down CPU performance for certain audio and speech tasks, leading to noticeable delays and degradation. To address this challenge, we propose HyperDegrade, a novel optimization framework that streamlines audio and speech processing for both Intel and AMD CPUs, taking into account various hardware mitigations and their impact on performance. By leveraging a sophisticated scheduling mechanism and a novel approach to task parallelization, HyperDegrade boosts CPU performance for audio and speech processing tasks by up to 8 times, while also providing a flexible and customizable solution for developers to balance performance and security requirements. Moreover, our framework is compatible with multiple audio and speech processing libraries, including WebRTC, FFmpeg, and SoX, and can be easily integrated into existing applications with minimal code changes. By making HyperDegrade publicly available, we aim to facilitate the development of efficient audio and speech processing applications for a wide range of use cases.

In recent years, over-parametrized linear regression models have gained significant attention, and several theoretical guarantees have been established for their excellent generalization performance. However, the impact of over-parametrization on models with non-orthogonal features has not been extensively studied. This paper specifically investigates the scenario where the number of parameters exceeds the sample size, and it proves that the time series linear regression model can yield a small error when the number of parameters is only slightly greater than the sample size. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model's performance degrades gradually as the number of parameters increases beyond the sample size, ultimately approaching the optimal error bound achievable with a model of size equal to the sample size. This behavior is characterized as the model enters a "benign misfitting" phase, where the additional parameters do not significantly impair the model's performance. This finding is reinforced by numerical experiments and can be viewed as a generalization of previous results established for static linear regression models. This research also highlights the importance of selecting the number of time series lags to match the data's underlying characteristics. This paper's findings are relevant to a wide range of applications, including linear regression models with non-orthogonal features, sparse models, and low-rank matrix estimation. The ImageNet dataset has been instrumental in advancing deep learning, and its widespread adoption has led to the development of numerous large-scale neural networks. However, the static nature of the dataset's classification labels has hindered the creation of a unified evaluation metric for deep learning dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce the Dynamic Learning at ImageNet Magnitude (DLIM) challenge, a novel benchmark that assesses the impact of deep learning dynamics across various tasks, networks, and optimization methods. The challenge leverages the ImageNet dataset in a transductive manner, where the classification labels are treated as dynamic and the goal is to track changes in the classification performance over time. The DLIM challenge provides a comprehensive evaluation framework for the temporal evolution of deep learning models, allowing for the comparison of different models and training strategies under dynamic conditions. The initial results demonstrate the potential of the challenge to reveal novel insights into deep learning dynamics and facilitate the development of more efficient and adaptive optimization methods. The DLIM challenge is open to participation and will be used to advance the field of deep learning dynamics. The dataset and evaluation code are available at https://dlim-challenge.github.io/. The challenge is ongoing, and the deadline for submission is 15 Apr 2024. The evaluation metric for the challenge is the magnitude of the change in the average precision (mAP) across all classes. The challenge is divided into three tracks: (1) the static track, where the goal is to achieve the highest mAP; (2) the classification track, where the goal is to achieve the highest mAP for each of the 20 superclasses; and (3) the generalization track, where the goal is to achieve the highest mAP across all classes using a model trained on a subset of the dataset. Researchers have created trenches in HgTe crystals with a unique structure, lacking a bandgap, to study quantum transport phenomena. By combining scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy with theoretical analysis, the team was able to investigate the behavior of Dirac particles within these trenches. They discovered that the energy range near the Dirac point can be divided into two distinct regions based on the trench width. In narrower trenches, a one-dimensional helical edge state forms, leading to a half-quantum Hall effect and robust zero-bias conductance. In wider trenches, a two-dimensional zero-energy state emerges, exhibiting a zero-bias cusp in conductance. These findings pave the way for further exploration of HgTe-based systems and provide a platform for studying topological quantum transport with Dirac particles. Moreover, the team's approach can be adapted to create trenches in other materials with a bandgap, enabling the investigation of quantum transport in controlled geometries.

In recent years, neural networks have been used to generate synthetic gradients for accelerated asynchronous distributed training. This method has been demonstrated to be effective in reducing communication costs and improving robustness. To create a system capable of generating gradients, we propose a novel approach utilizing Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs), a type of neural network that can mimic the dynamics of Hamiltonian systems. We design a specific HNN to replicate the gradient descent dynamics and experimentally verify its ability to accurately predict gradients. Our results show that this HNN-based method can efficiently generate reliable gradients for a range of deep learning models, including ResNet50 and BERT, and we also investigate the impact of model complexity on performance. Furthermore, we develop a method to train HNNs using gradient descent dynamics and demonstrate its effectiveness. Our research paves the way for exploring other Hamiltonian systems and provides a foundation for future work on HNNs in deep learning. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyang-wu/HNN-Gradient. Our findings are presented at the 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) is a critical task in Natural Language Processing, 
where a word with multiple senses is identified within a given context. 
Traditionally, WSD has been approached using supervised machine learning methods, 
where a model is trained on labeled data to make predictions for unlabeled text. 
However, high-quality annotated datasets are scarce and expensive to produce, 
making it difficult to train effective models. 
In this paper, we explore the potential of Context-Gloss Embeddings (CGE) in enhancing 
WSD performance. Context-Gloss Embeddings are a novel technique that combines 
contextual and gloss-based representations of words to improve the accuracy of 
WSD. 
We utilized a pre-trained language model to generate contextual embeddings and 
combined them with word sense gloss embeddings, leveraging the rich semantic 
information encoded within them. 
Our proposed method was evaluated on the Word Sense Disambiguation task for 
five frequent English words, using the SemEval 2010 Task 7 dataset. 
The results showed a significant improvement in F-score, with an average increase 
of 7.5% when using CGE. 
We also analyzed the impact of different contextual and gloss-based embeddings 
on the WSD performance and found that the optimal combination of these 
embeddings is crucial for achieving the best results. 
The proposed method was further compared to a range of baseline methods, 
including a state-of-the-art BERT-based WSD model, to demonstrate its 
effectiveness.

embeddings.

scarce gloss-based semantic information.

of datasets in future research.

multi-task learning, where the model is trained to perform both WSD and 
Word Sense Induction (WSI) simultaneously.

A significant challenge in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing lies in adapting existing models to new, unfamiliar databases without the benefit of training data. To address this, we propose a novel end-to-end parsing approach that leverages a supporting retrieval task to gather relevant information from the target database. This retrieval task is designed to provide a query that can be used in conjunction with the original input query to guide the parser. Our approach employs a dual decoder network to generate the retrieval query, which is then combined with the input query to produce the final parse tree. We evaluate our method on the Spider dataset and observe substantial improvements over the baseline models. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates the ability to adapt to new databases with minimal additional training. We also conduct an ablation study to examine the impact of various retrieval settings on parsing performance. To facilitate future research, we have made our code and pre-trained models publicly available.

We have developed a quantum hydrodynamic method that incorporates random phase-space factors and applies to interacting Bose gases in one-dimensional systems. This approach allows us to calculate hydrodynamic coefficients and phase-space distribution functions for such systems. We have demonstrated the method's effectiveness by calculating the hydrodynamic coefficients and the quantum distribution function for a one-dimensional Bose gas in both its non-degenerate and degenerate forms. We have also calculated the hydrodynamic coefficients for a one-dimensional Toda lattice and the one-dimensional Sine-Gordon model. The initial study of triangular flow $v_3$ in central heavy-ion collisions is considered a unique probe of the QCD matter's early stage properties. However, due to the complexity of extracting $v_3$ from experimental data, particularly in small systems like Cu+Cu collisions, a comprehensive investigation of triangular flow's system size and centrality dependence is required. Additionally, the need to understand $v_3$'s connection to initial conditions and collective behavior necessitates further study. In this paper, we examine $v_3$ in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200$ GeV using a transport model that accounts for partonic interactions and hadronization. Our analysis reveals that $v_3/\varepsilon$ exhibits similar behavior in both systems, with a dependence on transverse overlap area $\sim\sigma_{\text{recoi}}^2/4$ and a shift towards lower values as the system size increases. Furthermore, we find that $v_3$ in the most central collisions is driven by a combination of short-lived and long-lived sources, with the latter dominating in small systems. Our findings are consistent with existing data and provide a framework for interpreting future $v_3$ measurements in small systems. Moreover, we propose a new method to extract $v_3$ from two-particle correlations using cumulant charges, which is particularly useful for small systems and can be applied to LHC energy collisions. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the initial conditions and collective behavior in heavy-ion collisions.

In the field of computer vision, self-taught learning has become increasingly significant, particularly for tasks like 3D scene flow estimation, where extensive training data is not readily available. Although transfer learning via neighbor-based metrics has been employed to bridge this data gap, it relies on the assumption that nearby points in the source domain are analogous to those in the target domain. However, this assumption is not always valid, especially when the target domain contains novel objects or scenes outside the source domain's scope. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel Adversarial Metric Training framework that generates a domain-invariant distance metric without relying on the target domain's neighbors. This metric is then utilized to estimate the 3D scene flow in the target domain. Experimental results on the SIFT Flow and KITTI Scene Flow datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach over the neighbor-based transfer learning method. Moreover, our method achieves comparable performance to fully supervised learning on the SIFT Flow dataset and surpasses it on the KITTI Scene Flow dataset. Additionally, we conduct an ablation study to evaluate the impact of our method's components on the flow estimation accuracy. Our approach is user-friendly and does not necessitate any modifications to the network architecture or the optimization algorithm. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyang-ai/AdMiT-SCF.

Seismic source waveform inversion aims to recover accurate images of the subsurface by accurately modeling the seismic source. However, source waveform and structural recovery are highly coupled, making this problem computationally challenging to solve. A common approach to simplify this issue is source wavelet estimation, which assumes the source and structure are independent. This research proposes an alternative method, using a data-driven source time-domain waveform as a parameter in the inversion for the subsurface structure. We demonstrate this approach on synthetic data with a complex model, achieving successful recovery of the structure and source waveform. Furthermore, we apply this method to real data from the Marmous-36 experiment, recovering a source waveform that matches the predicted wavelet from full-waveform inversion and providing valuable insights into the seismic source mechanism. This research shows that the proposed method can recover both the source and structure from seismic data without making unrealistic assumptions. To improve this method, we discuss potential future directions, including the use of machine learning to enhance the source waveform estimation and the application of this method to more complex models. This effect is particularly pronounced when the superconducting order parameter has a specific anisotropic structure. We also examined the influence of an external magnetic field on the susceptibility, finding that it can lead to oscillations in the susceptibility as the field aligns with specific directions of the superconducting order parameter. This research focused on a specific material, strontium mercurite, and found that the temperature and anisotropy of the superconducting order parameter play critical roles in determining the magnetic susceptibility. This study provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the magnetic properties of a particular material and offers a framework for analyzing similar phenomena in other materials. Ultimately, our research reveals that by adjusting certain system parameters, the performance of non-coherent differential CPM detection systems can be made more robust against timing delays.

In recent years, video forecasting has become increasingly significant for applications like sports analysis and video games. However, existing research focuses primarily on 3D scenes and outdoor videos, neglecting the complexity of 2D videos featuring multiple characters. This paper introduces a novel perspective video forecasting approach, specifically tailored for 2D videos with multiple agents. We propose a dual representation learning framework, where two separate neural networks process the input video to generate two distinct future frame predictions. These predictions are then combined using a spatial attention mechanism to produce the final forecasted frame. We also introduce a custom evaluation metric to assess the temporal coherence of the generated frames. Our method achieves superior performance in the Perspective Soccer Forecasting Dataset, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. The inter-orbital interaction in rare-earth ions is crucial for their magnetic properties and has been utilized in the development of novel magnetic materials. However, accurately measuring inter-orbital interaction in rare-earth ions is challenging due to the weak nature of the interaction and the need for precise control over the orbital occupation. In this study, we successfully measured the inter-orbital interaction in Yb$^{3+}$ ions using x-ray absorption spectroscopy and found that it is as strong as 0.1 eV. This method combines multiple machine learning algorithms to accurately remove diffuse background signals from the data. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a comparison with a traditional approach, revealing a 10% to 20% reduction in the all-sky map's intensity above 50 MeV. Our research indicates that approximately 10% of blazars exhibit variability in their gamma-ray emissions, and we have created a comprehensive catalog of these sources for further study. This catalog comprises approximately 10,000 variable sources, including 7,000 blazars, and is available for scientific investigation. This study's findings highlight the significance of machine learning in astrophysics and the potential of the Fermi-LAT satellite for discovering variable sources across the entire sky. In a serial dictatorship, where one decision-maker takes turns with another to make all decisions, we examine the possibility of improving social welfare through a more complex decision-making process. We find that, in a wide range of scenarios, a more intricate method of decision-making, such as a pairwise majority cycle between two decision-makers, can indeed lead to a better outcome for both individuals compared to a serial dictatorship. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any Pareto-optimal outcome can be achieved through a pairwise majority cycle between two decision-makers with suitable preferences. Additionally, we explore the conditions under which a more complex process like a Condorcet extension is preferable to a pairwise majority cycle. Moreover, we discuss the implications of our findings for various applications, including those involving multiple voters, as well as dynamic processes like Sophie de Meritens' "Court of Rome" system.

Binary asteroids are a crucial area of study, offering insights into the formation and evolution of small bodies in our solar system.  Identifying binary asteroids is challenging due to the small size of these objects relative to the resolution of astronomical images. hinders the ability of automated theorem proving tools to work with them.

computationally active parts of the specifications. This is achieved by
converting them into the form of lemmas with a condition, which can then

The rapid dissemination of news on social media platforms has led to an increase in the spread of false information, posing a significant threat to individuals, communities, and societies. As a result, there is a growing need for efficient methods to identify false news. Traditional machine learning-based approaches for detecting false news rely on large datasets of labeled information, which can be difficult to obtain and maintain due to the constantly evolving nature of news. In contrast, transfer learning and meta-learning techniques have shown promise in adapting to new news without extensive training data. However, they often fall short in detecting newly emerging false news stories that have little to no online presence. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for the meta-learning of news detection, which leverages the benefits of both meta-learning and neural process networks to effectively identify both existing and emerging false news stories. The proposed framework utilizes a meta-learning component to adapt to the news distribution and a neural process component to learn the representation of individual news articles based on their relationships with other articles. The evaluation of our approach on a large-scale dataset shows its superiority over existing methods in detecting both existing and emerging false news stories. GP 2 is a high-level abstract syntax for general parallel programming, providing a solid foundation for the development of various parallel languages and their corresponding compilers. A GP 2 compiler can be viewed as a function that transforms GP 2 programs into equivalent sequential programs. However, the GP 2 framework's flexibility allows for numerous compiler designs, and the choice of one over another is not clear-cut. In response to this uncertainty, we present the Enhanced GP 2 Compiler, a straightforward yet efficient design that effectively tackles the challenge of concurrent programming's inherent difficulties. The compiler's design is underpinned by a novel application of the Simon's algorithm for concurrent if-then-else expressions, and its performance is demonstrated through the compilation of GP 2 programs written in C, Pascal, and Modula-3. The resulting sequential programs are then executed using a threaded virtual machine, and the resulting output is compared to the original GP 2 programs' execution on a simulated parallel machine. The Enhanced GP 2 Compiler's performance is found to be comparable to the original GP 2 compiler, and the code is available for public use. The GP 2 framework and the compiler serve as a foundation for further research into the compilation of concurrent programs. The compiler's design is also applicable to other languages with similar features. The paper concludes by outlining potential areas for future research. Recent research has shown that injecting structured knowledge into language models via knowledge base augmentation can be beneficial, but the optimal method for doing so remains unclear. In response, we developed a novel approach called the Structured Insight Infusion Learning List (SKILL), which selectively incorporates insights from a knowledge base to enhance a language model's performance on specific tasks. Unlike existing methods, SKILL does not rely on predefined graph representations but instead utilizes a simple attention-based mechanism to capture relevant relationships between entities. We tested SKILL on two large-scale knowledge bases and observed significant improvements in downstream performance, with gains of up to 4.3% in F1-score and 2.5% in accuracy. Furthermore, SKILL's efficiency allows it to be applied to extensive knowledge bases with millions of entities, making it a practical and scalable solution for enhancing language models with a broad spectrum of knowledge. In noisy environments, speech enhancement techniques can significantly improve the intelligibility of single-microphone recordings. However, these methods often prioritize overall speech quality over source separation, which is crucial for multi-microphone arrays. This paper introduces a novel end-to-end speech enhancement approach for multi-microphone arrays, prioritizing source separation while maintaining overall speech quality. The proposed Dual-Path Convolutional Recurrent Network (DPCRN) architecture combines the strengths of convolutional and recurrent neural networks to effectively capture both short-term and long-term dependencies in the spectral domain. The DPCRN is trained to minimize the combination of a source separation metric and a perceptual distortion measure. Experimental results on the multi-microphone DNS-RT60 dataset demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, with significant improvements over baseline techniques in both overall speech quality and source separation. The DPCRN achieves a 2.83-dB reduction in the average word error rate (WER) and a 1.53-dB reduction in the average source separation distortion (SSD) compared to the baseline. The DPCRN also exhibits robust performance across various noise types and array geometries. The code for the DPCRN is publicly available on GitHub.

A new approach to modeling atmospheric circulation is being explored through multi-fluid simulations, where distinct fluids represent different temperature levels within a stratified environment. By successfully reproducing the convection cell's stability and the associated heat transfer patterns, the model demonstrates its capability to simulate complex thermal circulation in a controlled environment. This achievement marks an important step towards refining the multi-fluid model and its potential applications in studying real-world atmospheric phenomena.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable performance in various tasks, yet their effectiveness is compromised when encountering unfamiliar data due to a lack of robustness. To address this limitation, knowledge transfer methods are employed to modify pre-trained models, enhancing their ability to generalize. However, these techniques require access to the model's parameters and a vast amount of labeled data for training, which can be impractical in many situations. In contrast, this research leverages a black-box framework to manipulate pre-existing models without parameter disclosure, utilizing only decision outputs for training. Furthermore, we develop a zero-shot knowledge transfer approach that enables the selection of suitable models without the need for exhaustive evaluation. Our method is applied to three distinct domains: image classification, natural language processing, and speech recognition. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showcasing improved performance on unseen data with minimal additional information required. The proposed method is also scalable, allowing for the transfer of knowledge across various models without modification. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyang-hu/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer.

In complex tasks, multiple agents with diverse capabilities can collaborate
effectively to achieve a common goal. To develop a single agent that can perform
such tasks, it would be beneficial to train it using a co-observation learning
framework, where the agent is trained on a mixture of its own actions and
observations from other agents performing the task. However, this approach
requires access to a large amount of data showcasing the desired behavior, a
challenge that can be difficult to overcome in many real-world situations. In
this paper, we introduce a novel co-observation learning method called
COLD-Net, which trains an agent using only a small amount of data from its own
actions and observations. COLD-Net leverages a dual-stream architecture to
learn from both internal experiences and external observations, and incorporates
a contrastive learning module to ensure the agent's behavior aligns with the
desired task. We demonstrate the effectiveness of COLD-Net through experiments on
a simulated robotic assembly task and a real-world robotic grasping task. The
results show that COLD-Net outperforms multiple baselines and yields comparable
performance to an agent trained using a large amount of expert demonstrations.

Neural machine translation systems typically employ encoder-decoder architectures with attention to select the target words to generate. However, the vast action space resulting from the probability distribution over the target vocabulary poses a significant challenge for reinforcement learning methods. To address this issue, researchers have resorted to reducing the action space by selecting a single word, often using the output probability distribution. In contrast, the current study leverages the entropy of the output distribution as a key signal to guide the translation process. An intrinsic motivation to minimize the entropy of the output distribution drives the model to generate more precise translations. Experimentation with the Transformer encoder-decoder model on WMT English to German and Czech data sets yields substantial gains in BLEU scores, averaging 4.0 and 1.4 respectively, when using the cross-entropy loss alone as the reference. Furthermore, the model achieves comparable performance to the baseline when using the Gibbs loss as the reference, demonstrating the versatility of the approach. The code is available at https://github.com/parthf/entropy-guided-nmt.

MongoDB is a widely used NoSQL database that has gained significant popularity in recent years. As a result of its ease of use and flexibility, MongoDB has become a staple in many organizations' technology infrastructure. However, MongoDB lacks a built-in mechanism to ensure transactional consistency, which is a critical requirement for ensuring data integrity across multiple document updates. In this paper, we present a novel approach to validate the transactional integrity of MongoDB using a formal specification language. Our method involves creating a formal model of MongoDB's transactions, which we then use to generate a set of test cases to validate MongoDB's transactional behavior. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to MongoDB's current implementation and identifying a previously unknown issue with MongoDB's transactions. Furthermore, we propose a solution to this issue and verify that it resolves the problem through additional test cases. Our research provides a foundation for developing a tool to automate the validation of MongoDB's transactional integrity. Our approach and findings are available online at https://github.com/ahmadrezaei/mongodb-tlc. Our research focuses on MongoDB version 5.0, but our approach can be adapted to other versions of MongoDB. Identifying distinct clusters in time series data from dynamic systems is a complex task, especially when the systems' behavior is influenced by exogenous events. This challenge becomes even more difficult when the systems' dynamics are non-stationary and the relationships between variables change over time. In such scenarios, traditional clustering methods may fail to capture the underlying structure of the data, leading to inaccurate results. This research proposes a novel approach called Impact Based Clustering (IBC) to address these challenges by utilizing the effects of external events on the systems' behavior to inform clustering decisions. IBC leverages data from multiple time points following events to create a similarity measure that assesses the change in relationships between variables. This measure is then integrated into a density peak-based clustering algorithm to identify clusters. The proposed method is demonstrated through applications to synthetic and real-world data from dynamic systems, including traffic patterns and social network analysis, highlighting the benefits of IBC in revealing meaningful clusters and extracting actionable insights from time series data affected by external events. The research also presents a computational tool for implementing IBC using the R programming language.

In recent years, generative adversarial networks have gained significant attention for producing coherent and realistic text, especially in scenarios where the opposing agent's model is unknown. However, training such models typically involves optimizing a non-differentiable objective function to create an opposing agent that can effectively generate text that is indistinguishable from a given dataset. This challenge is compounded when the opposing agent's model is sparse, which can lead to performance degradation due to the limited capacity of the model. To address this issue, we propose a novel training method called SparseGAN, which utilizes a differentiable proxy loss to train a generative adversarial model when the opposing agent's model is sparse and unknown. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SparseGAN through comprehensive experiments on the LM1R and WikiText-2 datasets, achieving superior results to the current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we show that SparseGAN can be applied to scenarios with an unknown dense opposing agent model, which we term as a special case of sparse models. To validate this, we conducted additional experiments using the Text8 dataset, which yielded comparable results to the current baselines. Program verification is a fundamental task in computer science, where we establish the correctness of software programs by confirming they adhere to specific rules and guidelines. Historically, researchers have focused on verifying programs after they are fully developed, but more recently, there's growing interest in examining programs during their development stage. This is particularly relevant in areas like artificial intelligence and machine learning, where programs are often generated automatically. In this context, program development can be viewed as a search problem for finding the most suitable program from a given set of options. This perspective has led to the development of methods for verifying programs by considering the underlying reasons for their behavior, which are known as explanation-based methods. These techniques compare the desired program behavior to the actual behavior of the program, and then identify the aspects that align with each other. This alignment is crucial in verifying programs, as it ensures the program behaves correctly for a specific reason. In this paper, we introduce a new concept called the program examination principle, which involves examining the underlying reasons for a program's behavior. This principle is geometric in nature and can be applied to various verification tasks, including checking the properties of functions, validating the correctness of programs, and ensuring the safety of systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this principle can be used to develop efficient methods for verifying programs, and provide a framework for combining these methods with existing techniques. This framework is flexible and can be applied to both artificial intelligence and machine learning programs. In addition, we discuss the relationship between the program examination principle and the concept of program abstractions, and explore the potential applications of this principle in areas like program synthesis and the verification of temporal properties. Finally, we outline some open research questions related to the program examination principle. However, due to the excessive computational requirements, it's difficult to perform long-term simulations using high-resolution finite difference methods for the Einstein field equations. To overcome this issue, we propose a novel approach called the Cauchy-Characteristic Initial Value Problem (ICP) Tidal Taylor-Kreiss (CTTK) method. This method leverages the CTK scheme to solve the Einstein field equations in the context of numerical relativity, without the need for a pseudo-spectral method. By utilizing a compact scheme, we can reduce the amount of data required for the simulations. This allows us to obtain high-resolution solutions in the region near the merger, without the need for a large number of grid points. Topological phases in one-dimensional systems have been extensively studied, 
yet the impact of disorder on these phases remains poorly understood, 
especially for systems with spin-symmetry. In this research, we examine the 
effect of random on-site potentials on a class of one-dimensional spinless 
lattice systems near the symmetry-breaking point. We find that the systems 
exhibit topological properties in the presence of strong disorder, 
characterized by a non-zero topological invariant and protected edge 
states. We also develop a theoretical framework to analyze these systems 
using a topological winding number, and demonstrate the presence of edge 
states through numerical calculations using a tight-binding model. 
Furthermore, we investigate the spatial distribution of edge states in 
chaotic samples and find that they are localized within topologically 
distinct regions. We propose that such systems can be created in experiments 
using a Topological Anderson Solid as a model, and suggest that they could

To create a model that can generate high-quality responses to open-domain commonsense questions, we propose a novel approach that utilizes a combination of two distinct objectives in a sequence of question answering tasks. Initially, a coarse model is trained to provide a general answer based on the question alone, without access to additional context. This model serves as the foundation for a more refined model that incorporates a rich source of semantic knowledge, allowing it to generate a more precise and accurate response. Through this two-stage process, the model is able to leverage its own previous response as a source of context, effectively allowing it to tap into its own internal semantic knowledge. This internal knowledge is then utilized to generate a response that is more semantically connected to the original question. We evaluate our approach on the CommonsenseQA dataset and achieve a new state-of-the-art performance of 88.4% in accuracy, surpassing the previous best result of 87.5% obtained by the TAPAS model. We also conduct an in-depth analysis of the model's performance to better understand the relationship between the semantic connection of the generated response and the model's accuracy. We believe this research provides a foundation for exploring the connection between the semantic connection of generated responses and the model's accuracy in open-domain question answering tasks. We also propose a novel evaluation metric called semantic connection score (SCS) to quantify this relationship. We make our code and data available at https://github.com/ChengyueXu/CoarseToCareful.

The effectiveness of machine learning models can be significantly enhanced by incorporating diverse data, and it is particularly beneficial for models used in decision-making applications. However, when training models on multiple datasets from different sources, especially in a non-convex setting, the diversity of data can lead to obstacles in optimization, causing the model to converge slowly or even diverge. To address this challenge, we propose a novel random stroll method that efficiently combines diverse data for model training in a federated learning framework. Unlike traditional methods that rely on the smoothness of data, our approach leverages the diversity of data to prevent the model from converging prematurely. We theoretically prove that our method minimizes the population loss and achieves a near-optimal convergence rate under certain conditions. Furthermore, we conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate the superiority of our approach in various scenarios, including deep learning models and real-world datasets. The simplicity and efficacy of our method make it an attractive option for practitioners seeking to train machine learning models on diverse data. The code for our method is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuchen/Random-Stroll-Fed.

We establish that for a wide range of complex analytic varieties without compact components, the $\bar\partial$-operator does not have a continuous inverse on the space of square-integrable functions. This conclusion applies to domains in $\mathbb{C}^n$, non-compact domains with finite number of connected components in $\mathbb{C}^n$, and domains within the unit disk in $\mathbb{C}^n$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the absence of a compact component is a necessary condition for the $\bar\partial$-involutivity. This condition is met for domains with the property of finite type, but not satisfied for domains with the Hartogs' hole. Additionally, we provide a characterization of the varieties where the $\bar\partial$-operator has a continuous inverse on $L^2$ functions as those with compact closure. This characterization is utilized to demonstrate the non-existence of locally holomorphic functions on certain varieties with the property of finite type. Finally, we establish that the $\bar\partial$-operator does not have a continuous inverse on the space of square-integrable functions on the set of the zero locus of a single holomorphic function outside its zero set. This result is then applied to demonstrate the non-existence of locally holomorphic functions on varieties with the property of finite type and the non-existence of locally holomorphic functions on the zero locus of a single holomorphic function outside its zero set. This non-existence is also demonstrated through another approach using the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem. This research was supported by the NSF grant DMS-1603051. The complexity of proof formats in Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT) solvers has been a significant obstacle for several years, hindering the development of efficient learning-to-certify algorithms for deep neural networks. Although various proof formats have been proposed, they are often highly specialized and solver-specific, leading to difficulties in creating a general method for certifying deep neural networks. In an effort to address this challenge, we have developed a new approach that focuses on creating a universal format for SMT proofs, rather than optimizing individual proof formats. Our method, which we call "lazy" certification, involves a simple and efficient algorithm that learns from deep neural network mistakes by using a general proof format as a guide. We have tested this approach on a range of datasets and solvers, using a proposed universal proof format called Alethe, and the results show that it is highly effective in certifying deep neural networks. Our findings suggest that the need for a universal proof format is more critical than the need for an optimized proof format, and we believe that our work has significant implications for the field of artificial intelligence. Our research has been made publicly available on our website.

Recent studies have shown that neural transfer learning can significantly improve
speech recognition performance. However, the majority of existing research focuses
on transfer learning within the same language and with the same level of
abstraction. In this paper, we explore two novel transfer learning scenarios:
1) transferring from a coarser level of abstraction to a more detailed one, and
2) transferring across different languages at the same level of abstraction. We
propose a novel method to select the optimal intermediate target network for
both scenarios, which is validated through experiments on the Librispeech corpus
and shows improved performance. Furthermore, we apply this method to transfer
learning across languages and achieve state-of-the-art results on the English
Librispeech dataset and the German AISHELL-1 dataset. Our code is publicly
available on GitHub.

Offline reinforcement learning enables the utilization of existing datasets for training agents without the need for a simulator. However, the effectiveness of offline learning is significantly compromised when only considering positive agent trajectories, as they lack the contrast provided by negative experiences. This limitation becomes even more pronounced in offline multi-agent reinforcement learning settings, where the interplay between multiple interacting agents can lead to complex dynamics and unstable equilibria. In such scenarios, the absence of contrasting experiences can cause the agent to become stuck in suboptimal equilibria. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a new offline learning framework that can handle positive trajectories in multi-agent reinforcement learning settings. The proposed approach leverages a specially designed equilibrium critic and a peer-to-peer multi-agent learning architecture to efficiently learn from positive trajectories. Experimental evaluations conducted on a range of complex multi-agent scenarios have demonstrated the superiority of our approach over existing methods. Cross-lingual word representation learning enables the transfer of knowledge between languages without prior knowledge of the target language. However, existing methods typically rely on bilingual data, which is not universally available. In contrast, multi-lingual shared semantic framework learning leverages multiple languages simultaneously, without the need for bilingual data. This approach assumes that multiple languages share a common semantic framework, which can be represented as a high-dimensional subspace. Recent methods use various optimization techniques to learn this shared subspace, but they often fail to consider the inherent structure of the semantic framework. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to create a cluster-consistent word representation framework, which assumes that words in each language are organized into multiple semantic clusters. Our method employs a non-parametric clustering technique to model the intrinsic structure of the semantic framework and a contrastive learning approach to learn a shared word representation that aligns with this structure. We evaluate our method on six languages using three cross-lingual tasks, and the results show that it outperforms existing methods in many cases. We investigate the effects of curvature on random surface growth models, specifically the Gaussian stochastic field $h(S^d_t)$ defined on the $d$-dimensional sphere $S^d_t$ with a fixed radius $t$. We derive an inequality that characterizes the variance of $h$ at a point $x$ on the surface, in terms of the geodesic distance $\theta(x, \omega)$ from $x$ to a given point $\omega$ on the surface. This inequality is then used to establish upper and lower bounds for the $L^p$ norm of the curvature of $h$ in terms of the $L^p$ norm of the field itself. We also examine the behavior of the variance of $h$ at points with maximum curvature, and derive an inequality that relates the maximum curvature to the surface area of the level set of $h$ above a given threshold. Furthermore, when the surface is the unit sphere $S^d$, we obtain bounds for the $L^p$ norm of the curvature of $h$ in terms of the $p$th moment of the field, which are sharp up to a constant factor. We prove these results by combining a specific arrangement lemma with the Borell's lemma, and we also provide some simulation evidence for the case where the surface is the unit sphere $S^2$. We believe that our results have implications for the study of Gaussian fields on curved surfaces, and we hope that our methods will be useful for other problems involving stochastic fields on manifolds. We also discuss some connections to the Brunn-Minkowski theory, the Gaussian surface area integral, and the Gaussian version of the Blaschke-Santalo theorem. Current GPU memory allocation techniques lack the concurrency required for efficient object allocation, leading to significant performance losses. To overcome this challenge, we developed DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator that enables the allocation of objects across multiple threads simultaneously, minimizing conflicts and synchronization. Our innovative approach employs a hybrid allocation strategy that combines free-list allocation for small objects and a binary search tree for larger ones, ensuring efficient memory access and minimizing fragmentation. Furthermore, DynaSOAr features a unique concurrent allocation mechanism that leverages a per-thread allocation buffer to reduce conflicts and a cache-friendly memory layout to optimize performance. Our experiments using real-world applications demonstrate that DynaSOAr achieves a 2.5x speedup over CUDA's standard memory allocation and a 1.5x improvement over a state-of-the-art concurrent allocator, while also reducing memory fragmentation and enabling seamless integration with existing programming models. Our findings also reveal that DynaSOAr's optimized memory access pattern results in a 10-20% reduction in global memory accesses. To facilitate widespread adoption, we have made DynaSOAr's source code available on GitHub under the permissive Apache License 2.0. Deep learning-based methods have been successfully applied to classify and detect lung abnormalities in these images. However, there's a pressing need to address the issue of data imbalance and bias in available datasets. Another challenge is the lack of regulation in sharing medical images due to privacy concerns. These issues are compounded by the limited availability of high-quality chest X-rays for training and testing. In response to these challenges, we propose a novel approach to preprocess chest X-rays using a classification-aware data augmentation technique. This method involves generating synthetic images that mimic the characteristics of positive samples, thereby counteracting the effects of data imbalance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in improving classification performance and detecting lung lesions on a small dataset of chest X-rays. Our method also exhibits superior performance when compared to other data augmentation techniques. Our research provides a foundation for developing efficient and effective deep learning-based methods for analyzing chest X-rays in the context of COVID-19 and other respiratory illnesses.
